regions.name: Middle East
overview: The Yemen war has moved from a coastal land-grab to a direct strategic confrontation with Riyadh: after taking the Yemeni side of Bab al-Mandeb, the Houthis struck the Saudi capital for the first time in this escalation on 19 September (a fire at a fuel depot near King Khalid International Airport) and are now fighting for the Kahboub heights overlooking the strait, with up to 169 reported killed in three days and more than 158,000 displaced in September alone.

The US-Iran war has shifted into a tentative diplomatic phase without any operational de-escalation: Witkoff and Kushner held a three-hour, Qatar-arranged engagement with FM Araghchi on the UN General Assembly margins on 22 September, but Tehran hardened its terms (a $24 billion single payment and a lifted Saudi blockade on Houthi Yemen), Hormuz transits fell to single digits a day, and Washington ordered a worldwide denial of services to Iranian airlines from 23 September.

Disarmament timelines in Iraq and Lebanon are slipping in public: Iraqi PM al-Zaidi pledged to Rubio on 21 September that militias would be disarmed by June 2027, effectively conceding that the 30 September US withdrawal date will pass with Kataib Hezbollah and Nujaba still armed, while Lebanon and its European and Arab partners used the 17 September Paris talks to seek a post-UNIFIL force before the UN mission leaves in January.

Israel is holding a steady, grinding tempo on every front ahead of the 27 October election: near-daily Gaza strikes (including a strike on a named Hamas finance chief on 23 September), continued ground incursions and checkpoints in Quneitra and Daraa that Syria's al-Sharaa condemned at the UN, and a new cycle of West Bank violence after an Israeli civilian was shot dead near Neve Tzuf on 20 September.

countries.name: Gaza
incidents: 19 Sep — Jabalia/Gaza City: Israeli strikes killed at least 3, including the son of Gaza health ministry director-general Munir al-Bursh near Jabalia camp, plus one man in Shejaia and one in a vehicle in Sheikh Radwan.
19 Sep — Gaza City: An Israeli strike on a motorcycle killed a Palestinian and wounded a child.
21 Sep — Northern Gaza (Yellow Line): A roadside bomb hit an unmanned IDF engineering vehicle with no injuries; the IDF responded with strikes on Hamas infrastructure sites.

23 Sep — Khan Younis/Gaza City/Deir al-Balah: An Israeli strike on a vehicle in western Khan Younis killed 2, including Mohammad Abu Elwan, whom Netanyahu and Katz described as a senior Hamas finance official; two further strikes in Gaza City and Deir al-Balah raised the day's toll to at least 4.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The nominal ceasefire continues to coexist with near-daily Israeli strikes and a casualty rate of roughly 15–25 killed per week; the 16 September Tal al-Hawa building collapse (21 killed) and about 3,000 buildings rated unsafe show that the humanitarian toll now also comes from the structural legacy of the war. The 21 September IED attack on an IDF vehicle and the 23 September targeted killing of a Hamas finance official point to a slow shift toward named-target strikes and possible militant attacks along the Yellow Line. Over the next 90 days, expect this pattern to continue through the 27 October election, with a real risk of sharper Israeli escalation if IED attacks on troops grow or hostage talks stall. A renegotiated enforcement mechanism is unlikely before a new Israeli government forms.

countries.name: Lebanon
incidents: 17 Sep — Paris: Macron, President Aoun and Jordan's King Abdullah chaired talks with European and Arab military chiefs on LAF needs and a post-UNIFIL force, possibly EU-led or Franco-Italian, before the roughly 7,500-strong UN mission leaves in January.

18 Sep — Bint Jbeil district (Chaqra): Israeli artillery shelling injured 2 as Israeli troops advanced toward border towns, including the outskirts of Deir Mimas in Marjayoun, and clashed with Lebanese soldiers before pulling back.

Mid-Sep (reported 19 Sep) — Nabatieh: Two back-to-back Israeli strikes hit the city and a third struck the ambulance team responding, adding to a UN count of at least 103 medical workers killed since 2 March.

23 Sep — South Lebanon border strip: Reporting documented widespread destruction of border villages in the Israeli-occupied zone, while prefabricated housing units were being installed for displaced families.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Israel keeps a steady campaign of air and artillery strikes and short ground pushes from its occupied strip in the south, including a tactic of striking first responders, while Hezbollah's occasional drone launches give Israel a stated reason to escalate. The main new factor for the next 90 days is the end of UNIFIL in January: unless a European or other mission is agreed quickly, a security gap south of the Litani will raise the risk of friction between the IDF and the LAF, and of Israel moving deeper to fill the gap. The LAF's 'Homeland Shield' phase two (Litani–Awali) is unlikely to move forward in practice while Israeli strikes continue and Tehran openly backs Hezbollah's refusal to disarm. An Israeli withdrawal within this period is unlikely.

countries.name: Iran
incidents: 17 Sep — UN Security Council: Russia and China vetoed renewal of the Iran sanctions Panel of Experts mandate (11 in favour); the panel expires on 26 September with no replacement mechanism.

21 Sep — Strait of Hormuz: A transiting tanker was hit by an 'unknown projectile' (2 crew lightly injured) and an LPG carrier was struck by debris, per UKMTO; Iran also claimed to have shot down a US Orbiter reconnaissance drone over the strait, while daily commercial transits fell to 1–8 against a pre-crisis baseline of 85.

22 Sep — New York: US envoys Witkoff and Kushner held a three-hour, Qatar-arranged engagement with FM Araghchi on the UNGA margins; the IRGC then demanded $24 billion in a single payment before negotiations and the lifting of the Saudi blockade on Houthi Yemen, and the General Staff threatened 'crushing and unpredictable blows' in response to any further attack.

22–23 Sep — Global: US Treasury Secretary Bessent announced a worldwide denial of fuel, landing and ticketing services to Iranian carriers from 23 September, after Turkish Airlines, AJet and Pegasus had pulled Iran flights until at least late March 2027; Iran also reported a 10.1% year-on-year economic contraction.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. For the first time in weeks the conflict has an active, if contested, diplomatic channel: the Witkoff–Araghchi meeting, Egyptian and Qatari mediation, and Trump's forecast of a deal after the November midterms. On the ground, however, Hormuz remains effectively closed and Tehran is raising its price rather than lowering it. Iran's addition of a Houthi-related demand ties the Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb crises together and makes a narrow deal harder. Over the next 90 days, expect probing diplomacy and a continued lull in direct US–Iran exchanges (no new coalition-attributed Iranian military deaths for 15 days), punctuated by unattributed tanker incidents and drone shoot-downs. A sharp relapse is possible if the US strikes the Houthis or Iranian maritime assets. The aviation cut-off and the 10% economic contraction increase pressure on the regime, and Mojtaba Khamenei's continued absence leaves unclear who can approve a deal.

countries.name: Yemen
incidents: 19–20 Sep — Sanaa/Saudi Arabia: The Houthis fired ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones at Riyadh, their first claimed attack on the Saudi capital in this escalation, and also targeted Bisha, Taif, Farasan and Yanbu.

20–22 Sep — Taiz/Lahj (Kahboub mountains): Houthi forces pushed into Al-Wazi'iyah district and along the Ras al-Ara coast to take the Kahboub heights overlooking Bab al-Mandeb and Mayyun (Perim) Island; up to 169 were reported killed in three days, and the Giants Brigades claimed to have killed Houthi Maj. Gen. Firaq Mohsen al-Asar ('Abu Saqr') and six staff.
21 Sep — Al-Jawf/Taiz/Saada/Marib: The Houthis reported at least 157 Saudi air strikes in one day; a separate strike on Mokha killed 6 civilians, including 2 children.

20–22 Sep — Washington/Yemen: The New York Times reported that Trump ordered and then called off US air strikes on the Houthis at the last minute; the UN put the toll since 6 August at about 674 killed and nearly 3,000 injured, with more than 158,000 displaced in September and over 3,000 fleeing by boat to Africa.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The battle for the Kahboub heights will decide whether the Houthi hold on Bab al-Mandeb becomes permanent: holding the high ground would let the group dominate the strait and Mayyun Island and threaten the remaining government-held corridor toward Lahj and Aden. Expect heavy ground fighting and intense Saudi air strikes over the coming weeks, with Houthi missile and drone strikes reaching deeper into Saudi Arabia, now including Riyadh and Red Sea export points such as Yanbu. US intervention remains the key uncertainty: last week's aborted strike shows Washington is reluctant, but another Houthi attack on shipping or on Riyadh's energy infrastructure could reverse that quickly. A negotiated de-escalation within 90 days is unlikely unless it is folded into a US–Iran deal, which Tehran's new Houthi-related demand now explicitly links. The humanitarian situation, with 18 million facing acute food insecurity and 90% of food imported, will get worse.

countries.name: Israel
incidents: 19 Sep — West Bank (south Hebron hills): Settlers set fire to an agricultural structure and sprayed graffiti inciting murder in Aghziweh east of Yatta, and cut the main water pipeline to the hamlet of Adqiqa.

20 Sep — West Bank (Neve Tzuf/Halamish, near Ramallah): A Palestinian gunman shot dead an Israeli man at a spring near the settlement; in a separate incident the same day, Israeli soldiers killed a Palestinian motorist they said had tried to ram them.
20 Sep — West Bank (near Jenin): Israeli forces killed a Palestinian during operations near Jenin.

19 Sep — Nationwide: Reporting highlighted IDF shortages of troops and equipment after months of multi-front operations; days earlier the US administration had advanced a planned $2.8bn sale of 2,000-lb bombs to Israel.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The fatal 20 September shooting near Neve Tzuf makes a cycle of settler reprisals and wider IDF raids in the Ramallah and Jenin areas likely in the coming weeks, adding to settler violence that is already at record levels in the run-up to the 27 October election. Militarily, Israel is sustaining its tempo in Gaza, south Lebanon and southwest Syria despite reported strain on manpower and equipment, which US munitions sales partly offset. Israel reported no new operations against Iran this week, and it is likely to stay in a supporting role while US–Iran contacts continue. The election remains the main variable over the next 90 days: a Netanyahu win likely keeps the current multi-front posture, while an Eisenkot-led coalition might seek an exit on Lebanon, but not on Iran or Gaza, within this period.

countries.name: Iraq
incidents: 19 Sep — Baghdad: A senior adviser to the prime minister said there is no fixed deadline for the militia-disarmament committee, formally separating disarmament from the 30 September US withdrawal date.

21 Sep — New York: PM Ali al-Zaidi pledged to Secretary of State Rubio on the UNGA margins that Iran-backed militias would be disarmed by June 2027; Kataib Hezbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba still refuse until all foreign troops have left, and a proposed 90-day ceasefire period before any weapons handover would delay things further.

22 Sep — Iraq/New York: Iraq began enforcing the US denial of services to Iranian airlines, while al-Zaidi joined Trump's meeting with regional leaders; Iraq's ground forces commander also called on the Yazidi YBS militia to disarm.

23 Sep — Northern Iraq: The US withdrawal stayed on track for 30 September, with the several hundred remaining troops in the north mostly moving to Jordan and other regional bases; Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, shut on 11 September after a drone attack launched from Maysan, restarted on 22 September.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. With disarmament now formally pushed back to June 2027, the 30 September US departure will pass without the core Iran-aligned militias handing over heavy weapons, which confirms last week's assessment. After the drawdown, the main risks shift: militias may claim credit for 'expelling' the US and turn their weapons on Kurdish and remaining US-linked targets in the KRI, and on Gulf infrastructure, as the Maysan-launched drone attack on the Saudi pipeline showed. Iraqi compliance with US aviation sanctions on Iran could draw pressure or retaliation from militias. Within 90 days, watch for a symbolic attack timed to the withdrawal, more strikes on Iranian-Kurdish opposition camps, and whether the June 2027 plan sets any verifiable intermediate milestones.

countries.name: Saudi Arabia
incidents: 19 Sep — Riyadh: A fuel depot near King Khalid International Airport caught fire and flights were heavily disrupted; the coalition said it intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile aimed at the capital at dawn, the first direct targeting of Riyadh in this escalation.
19–20 Sep — Bisha/Taif/Farasan/Yanbu: Saudi air defences thwarted further Houthi missile and drone attacks on civilian and infrastructure targets, including the Red Sea oil port of Yanbu.
21 Sep — Najran: A civil defence alert was issued and later lifted, with no impact reported.

22 Sep — East-West pipeline: The pipeline restarted at a low rate after a 9-day shutdown caused by an Iraq-launched drone attack, with full restoration expected to take weeks; Saudi exports via Hormuz reportedly rose to about 2.9 million barrels a day.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The 19 September Riyadh attack widens the Houthi target set from the southwestern border cities to the capital and to Red Sea export infrastructure, at the same moment the East-West pipeline, Riyadh's route around Hormuz, is only partly back in service after an attack from Iraqi territory. Saudi Arabia is therefore squeezed between a Houthi-held Bab al-Mandeb, a largely closed Hormuz and a vulnerable overland bypass. Over the next 90 days, expect a sustained, high-volume Saudi air campaign in Yemen and continued Saudi pressure on Washington to intervene, with MBS already lobbying Trump directly. Expect further long-range Houthi strikes on Riyadh, Yanbu and Jizan, and a meaningful risk of a successful hit on energy infrastructure. Iran's new demand that the Saudi blockade of Houthi Yemen be lifted puts Riyadh directly into US–Iran bargaining.

countries.name: Syria
incidents: 19 Sep — Southern Syria: The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights recorded 594 Israeli attacks on Syrian territory between 1 January and 19 September 2026, most of them in Quneitra and Daraa.
20 Sep — Quneitra (Tal Abu Qubais): Seven Israeli military vehicles entered the area before withdrawing via the Ain Zivan–Qudna road.

22 Sep — Quneitra/Daraa: At dawn, Israeli artillery shelled the outskirts of villages in western Daraa countryside, and a roughly 10-vehicle Israeli force set up a temporary checkpoint at the Rasem al-Halabi junction in central Quneitra, searching passers-by.

23 Sep — New York: At the UN General Assembly, President al-Sharaa demanded Israeli withdrawal, citing '500 air strikes, more than 1,200 incursions and 300 detentions', and said the Golan is inseparable from Syria while leaving the door open to peace.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Israeli ground activity in Quneitra and Daraa has shifted from raids toward a routine presence of checkpoints, patrols and artillery, strengthening a de facto buffer zone that Damascus cannot contest militarily and is now challenging diplomatically at the UN. No new Suwayda clashes were confirmed in open sources this week, but the ceasefire there remains fragile and flare-ups on a weekly or fortnightly cadence are likely to return. Over the next 90 days, expect continued Israeli incursions and detentions in the south, US-mediated contacts on a security arrangement that stay stuck on the Golan, and a risk of Israeli air strikes if Damascus sends forces toward Suwayda or the border strip.

countries.name: Egypt
incidents: 15 Sep (effects ongoing) — Egypt: Sisi hosted Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, pledged 'unwavering' support to Riyadh and called for secure navigation through Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb; Egypt reportedly rejected a Houthi offer of direct dialogue on shipping but did not rule out indirect contacts.
17 Sep — Cairo/Red Sea: Analysis highlighted the debate over how far Egypt will go militarily to help Saudi Arabia secure the Red Sea, as Saudi shipping is diverted north through the Suez Canal.
20 Sep — Cairo: Sisi met CIA Director John Ratcliffe on Egypt's mediation between Washington and Tehran, stressing a 'comprehensive settlement' and freedom of maritime shipping.
22 Sep — New York: Egypt took part in Trump's UNGA meeting with GCC, Turkish, Jordanian, Iraqi, Lebanese and Syrian leaders; no outcome was announced.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Egypt's exposure is still mainly economic and diplomatic, but it is rising: Houthi control of Bab al-Mandeb threatens the Suez Canal's partial recovery, even though Saudi traffic diverted north offers some offset. Cairo has moved closer to Riyadh politically while presenting itself as a US–Iran mediator, a dual role that protects its leverage but draws pressure to back Red Sea security operations with naval means. No kinetic incident on Egyptian territory was found this week. Over the next 90 days, watch for any Egyptian naval deployment to the southern Red Sea, which would make Egypt a potential Houthi target, and for canal revenue data. Egypt's Gaza mediation role continues in parallel.

countries.name: Jordan
incidents: 17 Sep — Paris: King Abdullah co-chaired, with Macron and Aoun, the military talks on support for the Lebanese army and a post-UNIFIL mission.

17–24 Sep — Jordanian airspace: No new Iranian missile or drone strike on Jordan was reported, extending the lull since the 9 September barrage on Muwaffaq Salti (18 of 20 missiles intercepted; an A-10 and about eight F-15s damaged).
22 Sep — New York: King Abdullah attended Trump's UNGA meeting with GCC, Turkish, Egyptian, Iraqi, Lebanese and Syrian leaders; no announcement followed.

Late Sep — Northern Iraq/Jordan: Most of the several hundred US troops leaving northern Iraq by 30 September are being redeployed to Jordan and other regional countries, increasing the US footprint on Jordanian soil.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The two-week lull reflects the broader pause in direct US–Iran exchanges while contacts at the UN continue, not any reduced exposure for Jordan. The redeployment of US forces from Iraq to Jordan makes the kingdom an even more concentrated host of US assets and therefore a primary target in any Iranian retaliation cycle. Over the next 90 days, Jordan will stay at a high state of air-defence alert. A relapse into Iranian barrages on Muwaffaq Salti, Prince Hassan Air Base or the Aqaba area is likely if US–Iran talks collapse or the US strikes the Houthis or Iranian maritime targets. The appointment of former military-intelligence chief Maj. Gen. Majdi al-Harasis as chief of staff points to a security-first posture.

countries.name: Libya
incidents: 17 Sep — Eastern Libya: UNSMIL expressed alarm over more than 30 extrajudicial executions in recent weeks; Libya Crime Watch documented 31 (23 in Benghazi, 8 in Derna) as of 10 September.

~20 Sep — Tripoli: The GNU asked the International Criminal Court to support its investigation into drone attacks on civilian energy facilities in Tripoli and Zawiya, which it describes as a 'broad and interconnected sabotage plot'.

22 Sep — Hamada/Zawiya: Petroleum Facilities Guard personnel shut a valve on the main Hamada–Zawiya crude pipeline, halting output at the Hamada and Tahara fields; the NOC warned of force majeure, the second such closure this month after 15 September.
23 Sep — Tripoli: Deputy Defence Minister Abdulsalam al-Zubi said there would be 'no release or deal' for members of the drone sabotage cell accused of attacking civilian facilities.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained, with risk indicators still rising within the band. Repeated coercive shutdowns of oil infrastructure by guard units, the drone-sabotage investigation and the eastern executions all point to armed actors using economic chokepoints and targeted violence as leverage, while the Dbeibah–RADA standoff in Tripoli is unresolved. The '4+4' election pact and US and Qatari engagement provide a political track but do not yet constrain the armed factions. Over the next 90 days, expect further valve and refinery closures and possible NOC force majeure declarations, with a plausible risk of limited armed clashes in Tripoli or Zawiya. A return to full-scale war remains unlikely.

countries.name: Tunisia
incidents: 19 Sep — Tunis: Hundreds protested for the release of four jailed organisers of the 2025 Global Sumud Flotilla to Gaza, held since March on money-laundering charges; all four are on hunger strike, one since 16 August.
19–21 Sep — Tunis: At least 11 protesters were arrested after the demonstration (activists said 13).
23 Sep — Tunis: International reporting on a jailed flotilla organiser's hunger strike increased scrutiny of the detentions and of President Saied's crackdown on dissent.
Ongoing — Tunis: Journalists continued to demand the release of Al-Qatiba editor Mohamed Yousfi, arrested on 4 September.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Arresting protesters in response to the pro-Palestinian flotilla campaign widens the crackdown from journalists and opposition figures to a cause with broad popular sympathy, which raises the risk of larger demonstrations. The death or medical collapse of a hunger striker could trigger significant unrest. Over the next 90 days, expect continued arrests under the 'false news' decree and financial-crime charges, recurring protests in Tunis, and persistent socio-economic grievances over water, power and medicine shortages. Saied's grip on power is unlikely to weaken. Border security cooperation with Libya is a secondary watch point given the instability in western Libya.

regions.name: Ukraine/Russia
overview: The strike war hit new peaks this week: Ukraine launched its largest drone barrage of the war on 20 September (Russia claimed 1,110 drones downed across 19 regions, 1,600+ around Moscow), timed to the final day of Duma voting and damaging the Moscow refinery, while Russia kept up mass drone-and-missile attacks on Kyiv region, Dnipropetrovsk and the grid that killed civilians including children.

A US-backed 'energy truce' is now the main diplomatic track: after meeting Trump at the UN General Assembly on 22 September, Zelensky said Ukraine is ready for a reciprocal moratorium on energy strikes, but the Kremlin has tied acceptance to protection of its seaborne energy exports and sanctions relief, conditions Kyiv rejects, so a deal is uncertain.

The Kremlin's political home front is locked down: United Russia won a record 355 of 450 Duma seats on a claimed record 59% turnout, including illegal voting in occupied Ukrainian territory, which gives Moscow a supermajority to keep financing the war despite fuel shortages and refinery damage.

Hybrid pressure and democratic backsliding continue along the periphery: Belarusian balloons shut Vilnius airport again on 21–22 September and an unidentified aerial object crossed into northern Moldova, while Georgia's ruling party packed the Constitutional Court as it pursues bans on all parliamentary opposition, and a heritage dispute has cooled Armenia–Azerbaijan civil-society contacts although the peace framework is intact.

countries.name: Ukraine
incidents: 20 Sep — Kyiv region: Russian drones hit 31 sites across five districts, 24 of them in Fastiv district, killing at least 4, including a woman and two three-year-old children in their home.
20 Sep — Kherson region: A Russian drone strike on a bus killed at least 3 people, including a 14-year-old girl, and injured 9.

22 Sep — Dnipro/Kryvyi Rih/Pavlohrad: Russia launched 212 strike drones plus Kalibr, Oniks and ballistic missiles at industrial and energy sites, killing at least 3 in Dnipro. Around 100,000 residents of Chernihiv region lost power.

22 Sep — New York: Zelensky met Trump for about 40 minutes at the UN General Assembly and said Ukraine is ready for a reciprocal energy-infrastructure ceasefire. He also asked for more Patriot interceptors ahead of winter.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Over the next 90 days, the key variable is whether the US-pushed energy truce takes hold. Kyiv has accepted it on a reciprocal basis, but the Kremlin's demands for protection of its seaborne exports and sanctions relief make an early, durable agreement unlikely. Until then, expect Russia to keep up mass drone-and-missile strikes on the grid, industry and cities (Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Chernihiv, Kherson, Odesa) as heating season starts, and Ukraine to keep up record-scale long-range strikes on Russian refineries and airbases. If a partial energy moratorium is agreed, it would likely be fragile and contested, with strikes shifting to military-industrial and logistics targets rather than stopping. At home, the NABU/SAPO probe and the winter air-defense gap (the Patriot request) remain the main vulnerabilities to watch.

countries.name: Russia
incidents: 17 Sep — Yaroslavl/Rostov-on-Don: A joint SBU, Unmanned Systems Forces, HUR and SZRU drone operation hit the primary distillation unit of the Slavneft-YANOS refinery and, according to Zelensky, damaged An-26 and An-12 transport aircraft and three helicopters at a Rostov airfield.

20 Sep — Moscow: In the largest Ukrainian drone attack of the war, Russia claimed 1,110 drones downed across 19 regions and Sobyanin reported 1,600+ intercepted around the capital. At least 3 were killed, and the Moscow refinery was damaged and halted crude processing on the final day of the Duma vote.

21 Sep — Nationwide and occupied Ukraine: The Central Election Commission said United Russia won a record 355 of 450 Duma seats on a claimed record turnout above 59%, in a vote that included illegal polling in occupied Ukrainian territory.
22 Sep — Samara region: Ukrainian special forces claimed a drone strike on an oil refinery along the Volga, and local authorities reported 1 killed and 4 injured.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. With a record Duma supermajority secured, the Kremlin has no domestic political constraint on continuing the war over the next 90 days. Expect Moscow to use the US energy-truce initiative as leverage, publicly welcoming it while conditioning acceptance on shielding its seaborne oil exports and on sanctions relief, and to keep striking Ukraine's grid through the start of heating season. Ukraine's record-scale drone campaign against refineries around Moscow, Yaroslavl, Samara and the south will keep refining capacity and the domestic fuel market (export ban, regional rationing) under strain and will test Russian air defense around the capital. Regime stability risk remains low, but fuel shortages and strikes on the Moscow region raise the domestic cost of the war.

countries.name: Belarus
incidents: 15–18 Sep — Grodno/Brest Oblasts: Belarus held 'defensive' drills along the Suwałki corridor near the Polish and Lithuanian borders, with mechanised and tank battalions training in border protection and counter-drone operations. This follows Lukashenko's 11 September order for rolling readiness checks of the army 'up to mobilization'.

21–22 Sep — Vilnius, Lithuania: Vilnius airport suspended arrivals for about three hours after balloon-type navigational markers were detected. The airport attributed the incident to a 'hybrid attack by Belarus', the third aviation alert at Vilnius in two weeks.

22 Sep — Minsk: Lukashenko said Belarus lacks the potash volumes to meet Trump's announced 'massive' potash deal, a sign that the US–Belarus thaw built on prisoner releases for sanctions relief has limits.

Late Sep–Oct (upcoming) — Russia/Belarus: CSTO exercise season continues with Interaction-2026 in Russia's Central Military District and the Indestructible Brotherhood and Barrier-2026 drills in Belarus in October.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Over the next 90 days Belarus is likely to keep playing a dual role. It will continue low-cost hybrid pressure on Lithuania and Poland (smuggling balloons, drone transits, migration pressure redirected toward Latvia) and visible military signalling through rolling readiness checks and the October CSTO drills on its soil. At the same time, Minsk will keep a transactional channel open with Washington (potash, prisoner releases). Expect repeated closures at Vilnius and possible countermeasures such as Lithuanian border closures. There is still no indication of Belarusian forces entering combat, but the build-up of exercises near the Suwałki corridor keeps NATO eastern-flank alert levels high.

countries.name: Moldova
incidents: 21 Sep — Northern Moldova: An unidentified aerial object entered from Ukraine's Vinnytsia region and crossed Transnistria and the Dondușeni/Briceni area before disappearing from radar near Tabani. Airspace was closed for 24 minutes and army teams searched the area.

23 Sep — Chisinau: Energy Minister Dorin Junghietu said the ministry has asked regulator ANRE to extend Gazprom-controlled Moldovagaz's role as gas supplier to Transnistria until 30 April 2027, covering the full heating season.
Early–mid Sep — Transnistria: ANRE raised Transnistria's winter gas-reserve target by 150% to 136 million cubic metres, due by 1 November. Hungary's MET Gas remains the region's actual supplier.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. The 30 September Gazprom contract expiry is less likely to trigger an acute crisis than previously assessed: Chisinau is extending Moldovagaz's supply role for Transnistria through April 2027, and Moldova itself has already contracted most of its gas from non-Russian sources. The main 90-day risks are a Transnistrian winter energy squeeze if the reserve target is missed, which Moscow could exploit politically, continued drone and debris spillover from strikes in Ukraine, and ongoing Russian influence and disinformation operations aimed at slowing Moldova's EU accession talks. Overt escalation remains unlikely.

countries.name: Georgia
incidents: 16–20 Sep — Tbilisi: Georgian Dream widened its Constitutional Court suit to cover every party that cleared the threshold in 2024, adding ex-PM Gakharia's 'For Georgia'. The move restarts proceedings and keeps the threat of a ban hanging over the opposition.

17 Sep — Tbilisi: PM Kobakhidze announced the closure of the State Grants Management Agency, calling NGOs in general an 'artificial phenomenon created for foreign intervention'. Pro-government media and officials also targeted a Council of Europe-backed seminar over alleged 'unauthorised grant funding'.

22 Sep — Tbilisi: Two new Constitutional Court judges, Goga Kikilashvili and Sergo Metopishvili, were appointed to fill vacancies, and critics warned there will be 'no more dissenting opinions' as the court prepares to rule on the party bans.

22 Sep — Tbilisi: Giorgi Kvitsaridze, who obtained footage of police violence aired by TV Pirveli in June, was sentenced to 17 years on drug charges that his family says were fabricated in retaliation.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Correction to last week's assessment: no national vote was found for 4 October 2026. The 4 October local elections took place in 2025, and the anniversary of that date's unrest is now the more likely protest trigger. Over the next 90 days, expect Georgian Dream to use its reshaped Constitutional Court to move toward banning UNM, Ahali, Lelo/Strong Georgia and For Georgia. The timing is still at the ruling party's discretion, and the threat of a ban is being used as political leverage. Also expect further prosecutions of opposition figures, journalists and whistleblowers, and a deepening crackdown on civil society and foreign-funded activity, including friction with the Council of Europe. A ruling that actually bans the opposition parties would be the most likely trigger for renewed mass protest and a possible upgrade to CRITICAL.

countries.name: Armenia
incidents: 21 Sep — Yerevan: On Armenia's 35th independence anniversary, Pashinyan said relations with Russia 'will inevitably change' as Yerevan normalizes ties with Baku and moves toward Europe. He signalled he would not object to closing Russia's Gyumri base, against a backdrop of Russian import bans and trade pressure.

Mid–late Sep — Yerevan: Azerbaijan postponed a Peace Bridge civil-society meeting in Yerevan 'until tensions subside'. The dispute began after Baku took foreign diplomats on a tour of Karabakh and presented Armenian monasteries as 'Caucasian Albanian', filed an Interpol claim over items from Dadivank and set up a working group on 'Albanian heritage' inside Armenia.

22–23 Sep — Yerevan: Pashinyan suggested ordinary citizens could take part in governing the Armenian Apostolic Church as the Supreme Spiritual Council met, escalating his confrontation with the Church leadership.

22–23 Sep — Yerevan/Washington: A US Deputy Assistant Secretary voiced continued support for Armenia's defence reforms, and Armenia's ambassador in Washington said possible participation in US sanctions on Iran is 'discussable'.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Over the next 90 days Armenia will likely keep moving away from Moscow (rhetoric on Gyumri and the CSTO freeze, closer US defence ties), which increases the risk of Russian economic retaliation and influence operations. The Azerbaijan track is under strain but intact. The heritage dispute and the postponed civil-society contacts show how fragile the unsigned peace treaty remains, and TRIPP construction has slipped to 2027. The Pashinyan–Church confrontation is the main source of domestic instability. Watch for Church-backed mobilization, further escalation in Baku's rhetoric, and Russian trade measures.

countries.name: Azerbaijan
incidents: Mid Sep — Nagorno-Karabakh: Presidential aide Hikmat Hajiyev took foreign diplomats around Karabakh and presented Armenian monasteries as 'Caucasian Albanian'. Baku then filed an Interpol claim over items allegedly removed from Dadivank, drawing Armenian condemnation.

Mid–late Sep — Baku: Azerbaijan postponed the Peace Bridge civil-society visit to Yerevan 'until tensions subside', citing anti-Azerbaijani rhetoric in Armenia. It was the first setback for the post-Washington-summit civil-society channel.

22 Sep — Baku: Flights by Iranian airlines to Azerbaijan were suspended ahead of new US sanctions on Iran's aviation sector taking effect on 23 September, although Iranian carriers said they had received no formal notice.
Late Sep (upcoming) — Baku: Israeli PM Netanyahu is set to visit Azerbaijan, deepening Baku–Israel ties amid the dispute with Tehran over flights.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. There are no kinetic incidents, but friction on two fronts has risen. With Armenia, the heritage dispute has frozen civil-society contacts while the peace treaty remains unsigned and TRIPP is delayed to 2027. With Iran, Baku's alignment with US aviation sanctions and the Netanyahu visit are likely to draw rhetorical and possibly economic retaliation from Tehran. Over the next 90 days, expect continued Russia–Azerbaijan normalization, a slow peace track with periodic rhetorical flare-ups, and heightened Iran–Azerbaijan tension. A shift to border incidents with Armenia or a sharp escalation with Iran would warrant a review toward HIGH.

regions.name: Sahel
overview: JNIM has shifted from economic strangulation to direct, high-casualty pressure on Mali's security forces: the 10 September Dioura camp assault (at least 100 FAMa and 5 Africa Corps killed per AFP; JNIM claims 150 killed and 93 captured) was followed on 18–19 September by an attack on a post on Bamako's outskirts and a kamikaze-drone strike on the Sévaré drone base, targeting the junta's logistics and its drone advantage on the eve of Independence Day.

ACLED had recorded 2,145 jihadist-related events across Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger by mid-September 2026, putting the region on course to exceed 3,000 this year — the highest level in at least a decade — while Burkina Faso's information blackout continues to hide much of that violence from independent verification.

Sahelian juntas continue to prioritise regime protection over counter-insurgency: Niger stripped five more exiled critics of nationality on 17 September (25 in total), Mali's Goïta paired calls for 'dialogue and reconciliation' with pledges to intensify operations, and external backers (Russia's Africa Corps; a US-approved $414m debt facility for Niger uranium) remain central to regime survival.

Sudan's North Kordofan front is heading toward a decisive clash: SAF claims to have retaken 11 areas west of El Obeid while RSF claims a victory at Abu Qauod and is massing near Sodari and Al-Mazroub, keeping civilian casualties high and Chad's eastern border on maximum alert, while in Nigeria bandit raids in Sokoto and a booby-trapped IED attack in Borno show violence persisting on both the north-west and north-east fronts.

countries.name: Mali
incidents: 18 Sep — Dioura, central Mali: AFP revised the toll of JNIM's 10 September assault on the Dioura army camp to at least 100 Malian soldiers and 5 Russian Africa Corps personnel killed; on 19 Sep JNIM claimed 150 soldiers (including two colonels) killed and 93 captured and released videos of detained soldiers, while FAMa said an air-ground operation evacuated two companies that had held the garrison.
18–19 Sep — Bamako outskirts: JNIM fighters attacked a security post on the periphery of the capital during the night, part of a two-pronged operation.
19 Sep — Sévaré, Mopti region: JNIM struck a military drone base with kamikaze drones, targeting a key central chokepoint and the army's drone capability; Goïta convened a crisis meeting on 20 Sep.

21–22 Sep — Bamako: On the eve of the 66th Independence Day, Goïta called for 'dialogue and reconciliation' while pledging to intensify military operations; the 22 Sep parade went ahead amid heightened security, a week after more than 900 escorted fuel tankers reached the capital on 14 Sep.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained, escalating. JNIM is likely to sustain its current dual-track campaign over the next 90 days: continued fuel-blockade interdiction on the western and southern corridors combined with a growing tempo of direct assaults on isolated garrisons (Dioura model), probing attacks on Bamako's periphery and stand-off drone strikes against FAMa/Africa Corps drone and logistics hubs such as Sévaré. The junta will almost certainly respond with intensified air and drone strikes and escorted mass convoys, which can keep Bamako supplied but not restore control of the countryside; heavy losses and the captured-soldier videos raise the risk of internal military discontent. Expect further large-scale attacks on central and western garrisons, continued pressure on Mopti-Sévaré, and possible JNIM leverage of prisoners for exchanges or propaganda; a direct assault on central Bamako remains unlikely but periphery attacks are a realistic possibility.

countries.name: Niger
incidents: 17 Sep — Niamey: Tiani signed a decree provisionally stripping five exiled critics of Nigerien nationality, including former Prime Minister Ouhoumoudou Mahamadou, bringing the total under the 2024 order to 25; Human Rights Watch (22 Sep) called for the decree to be revoked.

17 Sep — Niamey/Washington: The US approved a debt facility of up to $414 million for Global Atomic's uranium mining project in Niger, a notable Western economic re-engagement with the junta weeks after the failed mutiny.

Ongoing — Niamey: The purge following the 28–29 August coup attempt continues, with dozens of soldiers and officials detained and the new chief of staff, Brig. Gen. Mamane Sani Kiaou (appointed 11 Sep), consolidating command; Russia's Africa Corps, whose drones helped suppress the mutiny, remains central to regime protection.

Ongoing — Tillabéri: No specific dated attack was verified for 17–24 Sep, but ACLED data (16 Sep) shows jihadist violence across the central Sahel on a record trajectory, with Tillabéri the deadliest single area.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Over the next 90 days the junta will almost certainly continue consolidating power through purges, nationality-stripping and prosecution of journalists and exiled critics, relying on Africa Corps for regime security, while courting selective economic partners (uranium financing) to ease fiscal pressure. This approach is likely to keep Niamey stable in the short term but deepens grievances within the officer corps, keeping a further coup attempt a realistic possibility. With security resources partly diverted to regime protection, JNIM and IS Sahel pressure in Tillabéri, Dosso and along the Benin/Burkina borders is expected to continue at a high tempo, with periodic mass-casualty attacks on army and militia posts.

countries.name: Burkina Faso
incidents: 17–24 Sep — Nationwide: The reporting blackout persisted; no verified, dated security incident was located in major wire services or regional outlets for this window — an information-vacuum indicator rather than a sign of calm.

16 Sep — Sahel-wide: ACLED data showed 2,145 jihadist-related events in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger so far in 2026, on track to exceed 3,000 by year-end; Burkina Faso remains a core theatre, including a February JNIM offensive of 30+ attacks that killed over 120 soldiers, rangers and VDP.
Background — Sebba/Titao/Djibo axis: Government forces continue to claim offensive gains against JNIM-affiliated fighters, claims that remain difficult to independently verify.
Background — Eastern border/W-Arly-Pendjari: The tri-border park complex with Niger and Benin remains a key transit and staging zone for armed groups expanding toward coastal West Africa.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Given the persistent absence of verifiable reporting and the region-wide ACLED trend, the JNIM-versus-IS Sahel contest for Liptako-Gourma and the sieges of Djibo, Sebba and Titao should be assumed to continue at a high tempo through the next 90 days, with JNIM likely to replicate the large garrison assaults seen in Mali. Government claims of battlefield gains should be treated cautiously. Analysts should rely on proxy indicators — satellite imagery, displacement data, and cross-border reporting from Mali, Niger, Ghana, Togo and Benin — and watch for renewed JNIM offensives in the East and Boucle du Mouhoun regions and for any signs of internal instability in Ouagadougou.

countries.name: Sudan
incidents: 17 Sep — North Kordofan: SAF said it retook 11 areas west of El Obeid after heavy fighting, including Kajmar, Sharshar and the area around Al-Mazroub along the Forty Days Road corridor, and pursued retreating RSF fighters toward the Darfur border.

20–21 Sep — Umm Badr, North Kordofan: An RSF attack on a gold-mining market killed 5 miners and wounded 27, according to the Dar Hamar Emergency Committee; a large build-up of SAF and RSF forces is reported around Sodari and Al-Mazroub ahead of an expected decisive battle.

c. 21 Sep — Abu Qauod, west of El Obeid: RSF claimed a major victory over SAF and allied forces, while SAF claimed gains in South Kordofan and repelled RSF attacks in Blue Nile; the US renewed calls for a 90-day humanitarian truce.

16–20 Sep — Al-Nuhud (West Kordofan) and Awny (Red Sea/Northern border area): Gold-mine collapses killed at least 82 and at least 10 respectively, highlighting wartime dependence on unregulated artisanal mining that finances both sides.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained, escalating. Over the next 90 days North Kordofan is likely to see a major engagement around Sodari–Al-Mazroub and the western approaches to El Obeid as both sides mass forces; SAF will seek to push RSF back toward Darfur, while RSF will almost certainly continue drone strikes and raids on markets, mining sites and infrastructure to sustain pressure on El Obeid. Competing battlefield claims make a US-backed 90-day truce unlikely to take hold in the near term. Expect continued high civilian casualties, further displacement toward El Obeid, Chad and South Sudan, worsening famine conditions, and continued debate at the UN Security Council over a nationwide arms embargo.

countries.name: Chad
incidents: 17–24 Sep — Eastern border: No new cross-border strike or clash inside Chad was confirmed in this window; the most recent confirmed incidents remain the 20 Aug SAF strike on a convoy in Ennedi-Est and the 27 Aug strike on a fuel market near Tine (12 killed).
13 Sep — Djaramay–Massaguet axis (near N'Djamena): Security forces conducted a large control operation, seizing weapons, nearly 200 rounds of ammunition, military equipment and motorcycles.
Ongoing — Eastern border: Chad remains at its highest alert level with around 100 armoured vehicles and signal-jamming trucks deployed near Tine; the border with Sudan remains closed since February.
Ongoing — Ouaddaï/Wadi Fira/Ennedi: UNHCR counts over 954,000 new Sudanese refugees in Chad since April 2023, with fighting in Kordofan and Darfur sustaining arrivals.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Over the next 90 days Chad is likely to hold its maximum-alert posture along the eastern border, seeking to deter SAF and RSF spillover while avoiding direct confrontation. The expected major battle in North Kordofan and continued SAF air operations against RSF supply lines make further cross-border strikes or incursions into Ennedi and Wadi Fira a realistic possibility, which would likely trigger renewed diplomatic protests. Refugee inflows will continue to strain eastern Chad, while Boko Haram remains a residual threat in the Lake Chad region and internal security operations around N'Djamena indicate concern over weapons proliferation.

countries.name: Mauritania
incidents: 17–24 Sep — Nationwide: No significant new security incident was found in this window; President Ghazouani began an inspection tour of the interior on 20 Sep.

Late Aug (background) — Nouadhibou/Atlantic coast: The coast guard rescued more than 300 migrants on 21 Aug and 161 more (including 17 children) on 25 Aug from boats departing The Gambia, after 143–144 people died or went missing on a drifting boat in July.
Ongoing — Nationwide: The EU-backed interdiction and deportation campaign continues, with rights groups reporting mass arrests and summary removals of migrants to Mali and Senegal.
Ongoing — Hodh Chargui/eastern border: Malian refugee arrivals continue amid JNIM's escalating campaign, adding to over 305,000 refugees and asylum-seekers, mostly around Mbera camp.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Over the next 90 days Mauritania will likely sustain its EU-backed maritime interdiction and deportation posture, with the Atlantic route remaining deadly and continuing to draw human-rights criticism. The main security variable is spillover from Mali: JNIM's escalation (Dioura, Bamako periphery) and FAMa/Africa Corps operations near the border are likely to drive further refugee inflows into Hodh Chargui and risk cross-border incidents; a direct JNIM attack inside Mauritania remains possible but has not materialised.

countries.name: Nigeria
incidents: 18 Sep — Minna, Niger State: Governor Bago imposed a 24-hour curfew after protests over the deaths of 37 suspected illegal miners, many of them teenagers, in NSCDC custody; mining was suspended statewide and the NSCDC state commandant suspended.
19 Sep — Kagara, Goronyo LGA, Sokoto: Bandits killed 3 people during a three-hour night raid; residents said 28 were abducted (police said 9, all later escaped).

21 Sep — Wumbi, Kala-Balge LGA, Borno: Suspected Boko Haram/ISWAP fighters killed a vigilante commander and booby-trapped his body with explosives, which detonated when CJTF members and residents recovered it, killing 4 more and injuring scores.

22 Sep — Sokoto/Katsina: Premium Times reported continued bandit attacks despite local peace deals and military operations, including the 7 Sep Tofa raid (7–10 killed, up to 40 abducted) and rescues of abductees in Katsina and Kebbi on 14–16 Sep.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Over the next 90 days north-west banditry in Sokoto, Zamfara, Katsina and Kaduna is expected to continue at a high tempo, with local peace deals failing to stop kidnap-for-ransom raids and Bello Turji-linked networks remaining a key driver. In the north-east, the reported JAS ceasefire does not cover ISWAP, and the IED-rigged attack in Kala-Balge shows continued capability for lethal attacks near the Cameroon border; ISWAP reprisal attacks on bases and CJTF remain likely. Civil unrest over security-force abuses (Minna) and the approaching election cycle add a domestic stability risk.

regions.name: Asia-Pacific
overview: The Pakistan-Afghanistan front reopened as the region's most acute escalation risk: the 18–19 September Kohat police-complex assault (31 killed) was followed by Pakistani airstrikes in Kunar and Paktika on 21 September, artillery duels in Kurram and the downing of eight drones launched from Afghan territory on 23 September, ending a roughly three-month lull while the Baloch insurgency continued in parallel.

China's South China Sea coercion crossed into physical contact again: a China Coast Guard cutter deliberately rammed the Philippine fisheries vessel BRP Datu Magat Salamat off Palawan on 18 September, which Manila called the closest-to-shore ramming yet, one week after Beijing's Scarborough Shoal 'nature reserve' declaration, prompting Manila to develop deterrence 'options'.

Great-power diplomacy is now overlaying the regional flashpoints: Xi Jinping's 23–25 September state visit to Washington, with a trade-truce extension to January 2027 and Taiwan arms sales on the agenda, creates short-term incentives for Beijing to avoid large-scale drills around Taiwan, while grey-zone pressure at sea and on Taiwan's outlying islands continues and allies watch for any US concessions.

North Korea accelerated weapons development while Seoul pursued diplomacy: the 20 September hypersonic Hwasongpho-11Ma-1 test (two launches) and the 22 September test of extended-range guided 240mm rockets aimed at the 'southern border' came as President Lee used the UN General Assembly to push for a Trump-Kim summit, confirming that Pyongyang is building leverage rather than pausing for talks.

countries.name: North Korea
incidents: 20 Sep — East coast: North Korea fired two short-range ballistic missiles toward the East Sea about three hours apart, its second launch event in roughly a week; Seoul's National Security Council called it a direct violation of UN Security Council resolutions.

20 Sep — Missile General Bureau test: KCNA said Kim Jong Un observed the test of a 'new weapon' assessed as an upgraded Hwasongpho-11Ma-1 hypersonic SRBM; Kim said it would give adversaries 'an incurable headache', signalling a move from research to operational deployment.

22 Sep — Near the inter-Korean border: North Korea test-fired upgraded 240mm guided multiple-rocket-launcher shells with autonomous precision guidance and claimed ranges of 100 km (ballistic) to 115 km (gliding mode), which officials said would shift firepower readiness on the 'southern border' (reported by KCNA on 24 Sep).
Ongoing — 2026 tempo: North Korea has now launched at least 15 ballistic missiles and other projectiles on nine occasions this year, versus five missiles on four occasions in all of 2025.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Over the next 90 days, expect Pyongyang to continue a compressed testing cycle, including hypersonic SRBMs, precision-guided long-range artillery aimed at the Seoul metropolitan area and possibly longer-range systems, timed to allied drills and to Xi-Trump and APEC-window diplomacy. Kim is likely to treat a Trump summit as an opportunity to secure de facto nuclear-state recognition rather than as a reason to pause testing, while continuing naval commissioning, DMZ fortification and military cooperation with Russia. A nuclear test remains a low-probability but high-impact wildcard; the more likely path is steady qualitative upgrades to tactical nuclear-capable delivery systems.

countries.name: Myanmar
incidents: 17–18 Sep — Kachin State: Kachin Independence Army-led forces continued attacks on junta river convoys between Bhamo (Banmaw) and Shweku and on 18 Sep reportedly captured a border base in Kawnglanpu Township held by two junta battalions, following the reported downing of a junta Y-12 aircraft on 16 Sep.

18 Sep — Magway Region: Resistance forces detonated an improvised 500-pound bomb against a junta convoy of 30–50 troops, reportedly killing at least 7 soldiers, as conscript-heavy junta columns suffer mounting attrition.
20 Sep — Rakhine State (Rathedaung, Pauktaw, Ponnagyun): Junta attacks on residential villages killed four civilians, including three women, in a single day.

23 Sep — Phat Kya village, Ponnagyun Township, Rakhine State: Three junta jet fighters dropped six bombs at around 01:48, killing two villagers, as the Arakan Army presses its counter-offensive around Sittwe after capturing at least six outposts on the city's periphery.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained, deteriorating. Over the next 90 days, expect the junta to rely increasingly on air power against civilian areas in Rakhine, Sagaing, Karenni and Kachin as its ground forces, now heavily reliant on raw conscripts, lose outposts, river convoys and aircraft. The Arakan Army is likely to tighten pressure on the Sittwe and Kyaukphyu enclaves while the KIA contests the Bhamo axis; a junta breakthrough is unlikely, but so is a negotiated de-escalation. Civilian casualties from air strikes and displacement will remain high, with further mass-casualty strikes on schools, markets and displacement sites likely.

countries.name: Pakistan
incidents: 18 Sep — Kohat, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa: A suicide vehicle bomb struck the mosque of the Old Police Lines complex, followed by a gun assault and a 22-hour battle; 31 people were killed (including 15 personnel and 6 civilians) and 103 injured. Ittihad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan, the Hafiz Gul Bahadur-led alliance of Pakistani Taliban offshoots, claimed the attack, the deadliest on a KP police complex since 2023.
20 Sep — Hangu district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa: Militants ambushed a security-forces convoy, killing six soldiers including two officers; ISPR said eight attackers were killed.

21–23 Sep — Afghan border: Pakistani jets struck what Islamabad called TTP and Jamaat-ul-Ahrar hideouts in Nurgal (Kunar) and Barmal (Paktika), ending a nearly three-month lull; Afghan officials reported three civilians killed and the Taliban vowed an 'appropriate response'. Artillery exchanges followed in the Kurram sector on 22 Sep, and on 23 Sep Pakistan said it shot down eight drones launched from Afghanistan near Torkham and Kohat.

13–20 Sep — Balochistan (Kech, Tump, Dalbandin, Kharan, Mastung, Khuzdar, Awaran, Quetta): The BLF claimed nine operations, including a 20 Sep attack on a military convoy and checkpoint in Pullabad, Tump, as the Baloch insurgency continued in parallel with the escalation in KP.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Over the next 90 days, the principal risk is a renewed cycle of Pakistani airstrikes and Taliban retaliation along the Durand Line, with further drone incursions, border-post artillery duels and possible border-crossing closures, as Islamabad links each mass-casualty attack in KP to Afghan sanctuaries. TTP-aligned groups are likely to continue complex attacks on police and army installations in Kohat, Bannu, Hangu, Dera Ismail Khan and Bajaur, while BLA/BLF operations against convoys and CPEC-linked infrastructure in Balochistan continue at high tempo. A mediated de-escalation with Kabul is possible but is unlikely to hold without verifiable action against the TTP.

countries.name: India
incidents: 17 Sep — Majalta, Udhampur district, Jammu and Kashmir: A joint Army, J&K Police and CRPF operation in the Brattal Sohan and Khubban forest areas killed two suspected Jaish-e-Mohammad militants after they tried to break the cordon with heavy fire.

23 Sep — Tamenglong and Kangpokpi districts, Manipur: Fresh ethnic violence killed a 36-year-old electricity lineman while he was repairing a 33 kV line, and 24 houses were torched in Makui Khuman and Makui Thanamba villages, most of them already vacant due to earlier displacement.

Ongoing — Manipur: The Naga-Kuki-Zo violence that began in February has killed at least 34 people, on top of more than 260 deaths and 60,000-plus displaced since the Meitei-Kuki conflict began in May 2023; Human Rights Watch has warned of renewed ethnic violence.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Over the next 90 days, expect continued lethal tit-for-tat attacks and arson along the Naga-Kuki-Zo fault line in Tamenglong, Noney and Kangpokpi, with highway blockades and attacks on infrastructure workers compounding the humanitarian situation; a durable political settlement is unlikely in this window. In Jammu and Kashmir, infiltration and encounters in the Jammu-region forests (Udhampur, Kathua, Doda) are likely to continue before winter closes the passes. Heightened Pakistan-Afghanistan hostilities add a regional variable, and New Delhi's posture towards Islamabad will remain firm, though no direct India-Pakistan military incident was reported this week.

countries.name: China
incidents: 18 Sep — Off Palawan, South China Sea: China Coast Guard cutter 21585 rammed the Philippine BFAR vessel BRP Datu Magat Salamat during a fuel-supply mission for Filipino fishers; Beijing's foreign ministry claimed the Philippine ship had 'ignored warnings' and accelerated ahead.

18 Sep — Beijing: On the 95th anniversary of the Mukden Incident, the foreign ministry used its press conference to warn against Japanese 'militarism', after China's defence ministry had condemned Japan's forward deployment of the US Typhon system during Orient Shield 26.

23 Sep — Washington: Xi Jinping began a 23–25 September state visit, his first in 11 years, with a rare planeside welcome from Trump; the two sides extended their trade truce to 10 January 2027, and Taiwan arms sales, AI, critical minerals and Iran are on the agenda.

Ongoing — Pratas and Kinmen: China Coast Guard patrols near Pratas increased earlier in September and four CCG ships entered Kinmen's restricted waters on 8 Sep, part of a sustained law-enforcement pressure campaign on Taiwan's outlying islands.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Over the next 90 days, Beijing is likely to use the Xi-Trump summit and a possible return Trump visit or APEC-window meetings to seek restrictions on US arms sales to Taiwan, while avoiding large-scale 'Strait Thunder'-type drills that would jeopardise the trade truce. Maritime grey-zone coercion, including rammings, water cannon, 'nature reserve' administration at Scarborough, Paracels construction and patrols near Kinmen, Pratas and the Senkakus, is likely to continue or intensify, because Beijing sees it as below the threshold that would derail US-China diplomacy. Relations with Japan will stay hostile around historical anniversaries and Japan's long-range strike deployments.

countries.name: Taiwan
incidents: 23 Sep — Tainan: As Xi arrived in Washington, Taiwan's MND spokesperson Maj. Gen. Chiao Fu-chun said the US government and Congress had 'repeatedly expressed support' for Taiwan's self-defence; a record $14 billion US arms package has been paused since the May Trump-Xi summit in Beijing.

23 Sep — Pratas Islands: Taiwan announced it is upgrading maritime patrol capacity around the vulnerable South China Sea outpost, including regular deployments of larger coast guard ships, after increased China Coast Guard patrols near Pratas earlier this month.

Ongoing — Kinmen: China Coast Guard vessels have entered Kinmen's restricted waters at least 24 times in 2026, most recently four ships on 8 Sep, while Chinese vessel presence around Taiwan reached a record 244 in July.
Context — PLA air activity: ADIZ incursions in 2026 are running about 52% below 2025 levels (1,200 aircraft from 1 Jan to 9 Aug), with pressure shifting towards naval and coast guard presence.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Over the next 90 days, Taiwan's main strategic risk is political rather than kinetic: the outcome of the Xi-Trump summit on the paused arms package and US declaratory policy. Expect Beijing to hold PLA air activity near the lower 2026 baseline around the summit while keeping up coast guard 'law enforcement' patrols at Kinmen, Pratas and off the east coast, with a risk of a large-scale drill if Taipei or Washington takes steps Beijing deems provocative after the summit. Taipei will keep pressing its defence budget (above 3% of GDP in 2027) and drone programme.

countries.name: Philippines
incidents: 18 Sep — Off Palawan, West Philippine Sea: At about 11:13, a China Coast Guard ship cut across the bow of BFAR vessel BRP Datu Magat Salamat at about 10 m, then repeated the manoeuvre and rammed it, causing severe damage to one side; there were no injuries. The PCG called it the closest to the Philippine coast that the CCG has ever carried out an intentional ramming.

19–20 Sep — Manila: Defense Secretary Teodoro called the ramming an 'unacceptable breach of international law' that the Philippines cannot ignore, and officials said there was 'no justification' for China's action.

21–23 Sep — Manila: Teodoro said the government is 'developing options' and crafting measures to deter further Chinese rammings, after China's 11 Sep Scarborough Shoal 'nature reserve' declaration and CCG water-cannon use near the shoal on 16 Sep.
Ongoing — Mindanao: Counter-insurgency operations against residual NPA units continue; four NPA members, including a regional leader, were killed in clashes in Esperanza, Agusan del Sur on 10–12 Sep.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Over the next 90 days, expect further CCG ramming, blocking and water-cannon incidents at Scarborough Shoal, Second Thomas Shoal and nearer Palawan as Beijing enforces its 'nature reserve' and tests Manila's resolve during US-China summitry. Manila is likely to respond with more escorted resupply and fisheries missions, publicity through transparency operations, and deterrence measures with the US and Japan, possibly including rules-of-engagement adjustments for government vessels. The risk of a serious-injury or fatal incident that triggers Mutual Defense Treaty consultations remains elevated.

countries.name: South Korea
incidents: 18 Sep — Seoul: President Lee Jae Myung said South Korea is continuing behind-the-scenes coordination to 'create an opening' for US-North Korea dialogue that could pave the way for inter-Korean talks.

20 Sep — Seoul: The National Security Council urged Pyongyang to immediately stop missile activity after two SRBM launches toward the East Sea, calling them a direct violation of UN Security Council resolutions.

22–24 Sep — Southern border threat: North Korea's test of extended-range guided 240mm rockets (up to 115 km), explicitly framed as shifting firepower towards the 'southern border', puts the Seoul capital area and allied bases more firmly within precision-strike range despite Lee's peace push.
23 Sep — UN General Assembly, New York: Lee called Trump's willingness to meet Kim Jong Un 'a hard won opportunity for change' and urged a resumption of long-suspended US-DPRK dialogue.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Over the next 90 days, Seoul will keep pursuing 'dialogue plus deterrence', lobbying for a Trump-Kim meeting around APEC and year-end diplomacy while completing the Ulchi Freedom Shield field events postponed to September and continuing trilateral drills with the US and Japan. Expect North Korea to answer drills with further SRBM, hypersonic and long-range artillery tests, which will strain Lee's engagement agenda domestically. The key risk indicators are DMZ fortification activity, any North Korean artillery or drone provocation along the border, and US decisions on scaling back combined exercises as a summit incentive.

countries.name: Vietnam
incidents: 17–24 Sep — Vietnam: No new Vietnam-specific security incident dated 17–24 Sep 2026 was found in available reporting; the items below remain the current baseline.

28 Aug (continuing) — Hanoi: Vietnam's Foreign Ministry formally protested apparent Chinese construction, assessed as early-warning radar sites, on Yagong Island in the Paracels and demanded that it stop immediately; the facilities appear designed to support the expanded Chinese base at Antelope Reef, whose first construction phase was completed by 19 Aug.

Ongoing — Spratly Islands: Vietnam continues its own build-out, with 534 acres added over the past year (about 2,771 acres in total), artificial land at all 21 occupied features, 15 harbours and a roughly 2,400 m runway nearing completion.
Upcoming — Hanoi: Preparations continue for Vietnam Defence Expo 2026 (10–13 Dec, Gia Lam Airport), with 128 companies from 31 countries registered, including US, Chinese, Japanese and Indian firms.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Over the next 90 days, Vietnam is likely to continue a dual-track approach: formal diplomatic protests against Chinese Paracels construction at Yagong and Antelope Reef while accelerating its own Spratly fortification, including runway and harbour completion. Watch for friction over Vietnamese fishing activity in the Paracels as the monsoon fishing season continues, and for Chinese responses to Vietnam's Spratly runway; direct Vietnam-China naval confrontation remains unlikely in this window given Hanoi's 'strategic priority' framing of relations with Beijing.

countries.name: Japan
incidents: 22 Sep — Yausubetsu Training Area, Hokkaido: US Army HIMARS and JGSDF MLRS carried out joint live-fire during Orient Shield 26 (8–24 Sep), the largest iteration yet with 3,700 US, Japanese and Australian personnel; Moscow called the drills 'categorically unacceptable'.

Mid–late Sep — Kyushu: The US Typhon mid-range missile system took part in Orient Shield for the first time and was deployed directly at a JSDF facility; Russia lodged a formal protest and China's defence ministry warned of heightened confrontation risk. The launchers are due to move to a US base in Japan around mid-October.

18 Sep — Beijing-Tokyo: China's foreign ministry marked the 95th anniversary of the Mukden Incident with pointed warnings about Japanese 'militarism' under the Takaichi government, keeping bilateral tensions high.

Ongoing — Senkakus and southwestern airspace: China Coast Guard patrols near the Senkakus continue at the near-daily tempo seen since 2025, and the JASDF scrambled against Chinese Y-9 intelligence aircraft on five consecutive days (3–7 Sep).
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained; watch for upgrade. Over the next 90 days, expect China and Russia to answer Japan's long-range strike build-up (Typhon, Tomahawk, SHIELD drone network in the Ryukyus) with more ISR flights, possible joint bomber patrols and naval transits of the Tsugaru and Tsushima straits, while CCG presence around the Senkakus stays high. The Okinawa gubernatorial result and the year-end revision of the three security documents will likely speed up southwestern island defence, deepening Beijing's hostility. A close-quarters coast guard or air incident remains the most likely upgrade trigger.

countries.name: Indonesia
incidents: 17 Sep — Jayawijaya, Highland Papua: Aris Sanda, a 41-year-old driver from South Sulawesi, was found dead in a burned car with a rifle cartridge at the scene; the TPNPB claimed the killing, saying non-Papuans who do not support independence 'aren't welcome'.

9 Sep (claimed this period) — Muliama district, Jayawijaya: Three civil servants from the Jayawijaya Agriculture Agency were shot dead; the TPNPB claimed responsibility and alleged they were intelligence agents, which police deny.

18 Sep — Jakarta: Human Rights Minister Natalius Pigai acknowledged that case-by-case responses cannot break the cycle of violence and called for a coordinated national response, as the killings renewed calls for peace talks; the Cartenz Peace Operations Task Force is investigating.
Ongoing — Central Papua: Security remains tightened around PT Freeport Indonesia operations in Tembagapura after earlier TPNPB attacks on convoys.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Over the next 90 days, expect the TPNPB to keep targeting non-Papuan civilians, including drivers, civil servants and migrant workers, whom it labels intelligence agents, as well as Freeport logistics and isolated TNI/Polri posts in the Highlands and Central Papua. Jakarta is likely to respond with more Cartenz task-force operations rather than a dialogue initiative, sustaining a cycle of low-level but lethal attrition and displacement. Calls for peace talks are growing but are unlikely to lead to formal negotiations in this window.

countries.name: Thailand
incidents: 17 Sep — Hill 450, Chong Sa-ngam, Phu Sing district, Si Sa Ket: The Thai Army said a dispute over Cambodian trenches and barbed wire that may have encroached on Thai territory was resolved through liaison talks, with Cambodia agreeing to fill in the trenches and remove the obstacles; Army spokesperson Maj. Gen. Winthai Suvaree urged the public to rely on official information rather than social media.

Mid-Sep — Border: Thai officials again urged bilateral talks and less provocation, saying Thai deployments are defensive; reported small-scale incursions (Chong Pling near O Smach; Hill 450) show friction along the ceasefire line. The US Embassy still advises against travel within 50 km of the border.
15–16 Sep (process continuing) — Singapore: Thailand and Cambodia opened UN-backed compulsory conciliation under UNCLOS over their Gulf of Thailand maritime boundary.

Background — Deep South: No major insurgent attack dated 17–24 Sep was found, after coordinated arson and bomb attacks at more than 50 locations in Narathiwat, Yala and Pattani on 23 Aug and a checkpoint attack that killed five rangers on 23 Jul.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Over the next 90 days, the Thailand-Cambodia land ceasefire is likely to hold, although local frictions over trenches, outposts and landmines will recur and be handled through liaison channels, with a small risk of a shooting incident flaring up; the maritime dispute moves into a slow UNCLOS conciliation track. In the Deep South, expect further periodic coordinated BRN-linked bomb and arson waves and targeted attacks on security forces, with no breakthrough in peace talks.

countries.name: Bangladesh
incidents: 18 Sep — Dhaka: Crude bombs exploded in at least seven locations, including Mohakhali, Jatrabari and Malibagh, between the afternoon and midnight, and a passenger bus was set on fire in Kafrul, Mirpur, after banned Awami League supporters staged a march in Gulshan-1 that police dispersed with rubber bullets.

19 Sep — Gulistan, Dhaka: Police broke up an Awami League flash procession at Stadium Gate No. 1; follow-up raids arrested dozens of activists (at least 74 over earlier Gulshan processions and another 32 this week), after International Crimes Tribunal death sentences against six people, including AL General Secretary Obaidul Quader.

24 Sep — Nationwide: Human Rights Watch warned that three laws passed on 6 and 10 Sep (an NHRC reform, an Enforced Disappearance Act and the Special Response Battalion Act, which renames RAB) reverse the interim government's safeguards and risk a return to enforced disappearances and extrajudicial killings.

10 Sep (context) — Chittagong Hill Tracts: The government gazetted three new CHT committees, including an Executive Committee chaired by the Home Secretary with military and intelligence members, which has raised concern among Indigenous communities.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained, with an escalatory tilt. Over the next 90 days, expect the banned Awami League to keep staging flash processions and low-level sabotage (crude bombs, vehicle arson) in Dhaka and other cities, especially around ICT verdicts and executions, met by mass arrests. The BNP government's rollback of rights safeguards and the rebranding of RAB increase the risk of abusive policing and polarisation. The CHT remains a latent flashpoint given the securitised new committee structure. An upgrade to HIGH would be warranted if ICT death sentences are carried out or the unrest turns lethal.

countries.name: Sri Lanka
incidents: 20 Sep — Nationwide: Reporting highlighted a surge in underworld gun violence, with 34–37 shootings and 17–18 deaths so far in 2026; police seized 867 firearms, including 14 T-56 assault rifles, between 1 Jan and 10 Sep.
21 Sep — Athurugiriya: Police arrested four suspects, including the alleged gunman, over two murders (17 Aug and 8 Sep); a live hand grenade was recovered from the suspected gunman.

23 Sep — Colombo: The 5th Director-General-level talks between the narcotics control agencies of India and Sri Lanka took place, following President Dissanayake's 9 Sep request for Indian support against drug trafficking in the Indian Ocean.
countries.coa: LOW maintained. Over the next 90 days, Sri Lanka's security environment is likely to stay stable at the national level, with gang-related shootings, narcotics trafficking and weapons circulation as the main internal security problems, handled through police operations rather than a wider security response. Security cooperation with India on maritime narcotics interdiction will deepen. No indicators point to renewed insurgent or communal conflict; a sharp rise in gang violence affecting tourists or public spaces would be the main trigger for review.

regions.name: Americas
overview: Explosive-drone warfare is spreading beyond Colombia's traditional hotspots: after the early-September ELN swarm on Ocana, FARC dissidents struck a police substation in Jamundi (Valle del Cauca) with around five drones on 20 September and a drone bomb wounded ten civilians in southern Bolivar on 23 September, with Colombian military data showing 439 such attacks since January 2024; counter-drone capacity is now the region's most urgent security gap.

US policy toward the hemisphere is shifting from coercion to transactional normalization with Caracas while keeping the military instrument active: Washington removed Venezuela from its 'failed demonstrably' drug list on 16 September and interim President Rodriguez pledged elections at the UN on 23 September, yet a 19 September Caribbean boat strike lifted the Southern Spear toll to at least 231 killed, and Peru formally joined the US-led 'Shield of the Americas' coalition on 22 September.

Emergency governance and austerity are converging into a new unrest risk: Ecuador's curfew in four coastal provinces coincided with the assassination of a judge and at least 23 killings in its first four days, Peru's president is framing crime as a 'war' after a gubernatorial candidate was shot dead on the campaign trail, and Bolivia's abrupt 83% diesel price hike on 19 September has triggered strike threats that test a state of exception banning road blockades.

Haiti remains the region's most acute crisis heading into the 30 September UN Security Council vote on renewing the Gang Suppression Force: joint PNH-GSF operations freed hostages in Kenscoff on 20 September, but school-run kidnappings in central Port-au-Prince continue, while Cuba's eighth nationwide grid collapse of 2026 on 18 September underlines that state fragility, not armed conflict, drives the Caribbean's second tier of risk.

countries.name: Venezuela
incidents: 16 Sep — Washington: President Trump removed Venezuela from the US list of countries that have 'failed demonstrably' to meet drug-control commitments, the first delisting since 2005, citing cooperation with interim President Delcy Rodriguez; Venezuela remains a designated major drug-transit country.

18 Sep — Geneva: The UN Fact-Finding Mission told the Human Rights Council that gross violations continue despite the leadership change, documenting 64 new torture cases since 3 January, 214 politically motivated arbitrary detentions (Sep 2025–Jul 2026) and an estimated 379–500 political prisoners.
19 Sep — Caribbean Sea: A US Southern Command strike on an alleged drug-smuggling boat killed four people, raising the Southern Spear toll to at least 231 killed in 69 strikes since September 2025.

23 Sep — New York: Interim President Rodriguez told the UN General Assembly that Venezuela will hold elections as part of a transition to 'full democracy'; the second round of US-backed government-opposition talks began on 15 September, with Maria Corina Machado excluded.
countries.coa: Downgraded to HIGH. US-Venezuela relations have moved decisively toward cooperation, with drug-list removal, accelerating US oil deals and a formal election pledge, so the risk of renewed US military action against Venezuelan territory within 90 days is now low. The main risks shift inward: the security and intelligence apparatus remains intact and continues short-term arbitrary arrests, the exclusion of Machado from the talks could fracture the opposition, and the absence of an election date keeps the transition open-ended. Expect Southern Spear strikes to continue in international waters without a Venezuela-specific escalation. Watch for an electoral timetable, the renewal of the UN Fact-Finding Mission mandate, any backsliding on press freedom, and disputes over oil-concession terms that could reignite political tension.

countries.name: Colombia
incidents: 20 Sep — Jamundi, Valle del Cauca: Around five explosive-laden drones struck the Potrerito police substation in an attack linked to FARC dissidents; no injuries were reported and damage was limited, and police activated the 'Plan Defensa' protocol.

20 Sep — Rural Valledupar, Cesar: Three men were shot dead in the early morning, recorded by Indepaz as the 92nd massacre of 2026, amid an Ombudsman warning over intensifying ELN–FARC dissident confrontation.

23 Sep — Mina Gorila, Montecristo, southern Bolivar: A drone-dropped explosive wounded ten civilians returning home after an armed group had forced them to transport wounded fighters; they were evacuated to Santa Rosa del Sur and the perpetrators were not identified.

22 Sep — Colombia/Costa Rica: President De la Espriella and his Costa Rican counterpart agreed to deepen intelligence-sharing against transnational trafficking networks; the military reports 439 drone attacks since January 2024, 173 of them in 2026.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Drone attacks are no longer confined to Catatumbo and Cauca: in this reporting week they hit Valle del Cauca and southern Bolivar and, for the first time in a while, injured a group of civilians, indicating proliferation of the tactic across armed groups and a lowering threshold for civilian harm. Over the next 90 days, expect continued weekly drone strikes on police substations and military posts, with further ELN–FARC dissident turf fighting driving massacres in Cesar, Cauca and Norte de Santander.
