The US decision to keep Colombia on the 'failed demonstrably' list adds pressure on the De la Espriella government to deliver visible eradication and interdiction results, which may lead to more offensive operations and retaliatory attacks. Watch for joint US-Colombian operations on Colombian soil and the rollout pace of the national anti-drone shield.

countries.name: Haiti
incidents: 16–17 Sep — Kenscoff: Haitian National Police operations reached several areas held by armed gangs for 21 months, according to Mayor Massillon Jean, though no casualty or arrest figures were released.

18 Sep — Bois-Verna, Port-au-Prince: Kidnappers seized at least five pupils and their driver near Lalue, prompting residents to block Dufort and Camelo streets; it follows school-run abductions in Delmas 75, Delmas 33 and Silo and the kidnapping of Radio Metropole journalist Wesly Renaud Jean.
20 Sep — Kenscoff: A joint PNH and Gang Suppression Force operation freed six people held hostage by gangs, part of the effort to recover captives from the August Kenscoff mass kidnapping.

30 Sep (imminent) — New York: The UN Security Council is scheduled to vote on renewing the Gang Suppression Force, whose initial 12-month mandate under resolution 2793 expires that day; the US and Panama are co-penholders.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. PNH-GSF operations in Kenscoff show the force can retake ground and free hostages, but kidnapping-for-ransom in central Port-au-Prince, including repeated targeting of schoolchildren, shows gangs retain freedom of action in the capital. Renewal of the GSF on 30 September is the most likely outcome given US and regional backing, although abstentions similar to 2025 are likely; a lapse or significantly reduced mandate would be a major negative inflection. Over 90 days, expect continued mass-casualty raids on peripheral communes, retaliation against hostages or civilians after security operations, and growing doubt over the viability of the 13 December general elections.

countries.name: Cuba
incidents: 18 Sep — Nationwide: The national grid collapsed at about 13:52 after the Matanzas–Cienfuegos and Matanzas–Santa Clara 220 kV lines tripped in unstable weather, leaving more than 9 million people without power; France 24 reports it as the eighth total collapse of 2026.

19 Sep — Havana: State utility UNE said nearly half of Havana customers had power restored via microsystems, with restoration elsewhere slow and some provincial areas reporting outages of more than 60 hours with knock-on water and gas failures.

19 Sep — Nationwide: Widespread public anger was reported on social media after the collapse; no large-scale street protests were confirmed in the window, following localized pot-banging protests in Havana's La Guinera and Fontanar in early September.
Ongoing — Nationwide: Before the collapse, UNE was reporting peak-hour deficits of about 2,000 MW, driven by fuel shortages under US oil restrictions and ageing thermoelectric plants.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained, under review. The 18 September grid collapse meets the trigger flagged last week for reassessment, but the government restored power fairly quickly and the collapse did not produce mass unrest, so an upgrade is not yet justified. Over 90 days, the peak of the hurricane season and continued fuel scarcity make a further nationwide collapse likely; the key indicator for an upgrade to CRITICAL is a shift from scattered pot-banging protests to coordinated multi-city demonstrations or a heavy security-force response. Expect continued rolling blackouts of more than 2,000 MW at peak, water-supply disruptions and rising migration pressure.

countries.name: Ecuador
incidents: 17 Sep — La Troncal, Canar: Judge Ramon Abad Gallardo was shot dead on his way to his office on the day the state of exception took effect; further killings were reported the same day in Guayaquil, Manta, Duran and Pasaje.
17 Sep — Puerto Grande, Machala: An armed attack killed three men north of the city, in El Oro province, where rival trafficking gangs are fighting over logistics corridors.

18–20 Sep — Guayas, Los Rios, Manabi, El Oro: The third night curfew of 2026 (00:00–05:00, until 30 Sep) began; by 20 Sep police reported 191 detainees and at least 23 killings nationwide, with gangs shifting attacks to the hours just before curfew in Duran, Daule, Pasaje and Machala.

22 Sep — Nationwide: Official data showed 5,676 violent deaths in January–August 2026, down 6.4% from 2025 on the back of falls in Guayaquil and Duran, but 2026 is still on course to be the second-deadliest year on record.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The curfew and 60-day state of exception are producing mass arrests, but killings have adapted rather than stopped, moving to pre-curfew hours and to peri-urban cantons in Guayas and El Oro. The killing of a judge signals continued pressure on the justice system. Over 90 days, expect the curfew to be extended or rolled over after 30 September, persistent violence in El Oro driven by the Los Fatales–Los Freddy Krueger feud, and more joint operations with DEA/SOUTHCOM support against Los Lobos and Los Choneros. Homicides are likely to stay slightly below 2025 levels but at crisis intensity; watch for retaliation against officials and prisons after high-value arrests.

countries.name: Peru
incidents: 20 Sep — Caraz, Ancash: Journalist and gubernatorial candidate Susy Isabel Aponte Polo was shot dead while campaigning at a market and five others were wounded; she had reported death threats, and no motive has been confirmed.

21 Sep — Lima: At the Armed Forces Day ceremony, President Keiko Fujimori vowed 'strong decisions' against criminal organizations, with 267 homicides (73% by firearm) recorded between 28 July and 14 September.

22 Sep — New York: At the UN General Assembly, Fujimori called for criminal networks to be designated as terrorists to allow greater military support for the police and announced that Peru had joined the US-led 'Shield of the Americas' coalition.
Ongoing — Lima: Extortion-driven shootings at bus companies continue (Virgen de la Puerta and Santa Catalina lines targeted on 10, 12 and 16 Sep); police data show 64 drivers murdered in 2026.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. The killing of a gubernatorial candidate is a new escalation that introduces electoral-violence risk ahead of the regional elections, and Fujimori's push to treat gangs as terrorists points toward a larger military role in internal security within 90 days, possibly through new emergency decrees in Lima, Callao and La Libertad. Extortion attacks on public transport are likely to continue at a steady pace and may provoke renewed transport strikes. Her falling approval (42% in September) increases pressure for visible, heavy-handed measures, raising human-rights and civil-military friction risks. Upgrade triggers: further attacks on candidates or officials, or a mass-casualty extortion bombing.

countries.name: Bolivia
incidents: 19 Sep — La Paz: Supreme Decree 5716 abolished the remaining diesel subsidy, raising the pump price 83% from Bs 9.80 to Bs 17.95 per litre, well ahead of the January 2027 date previously signalled; the subsidy was costing about US$55 million a week.

21 Sep — La Paz and Santa Cruz: La Paz interprovincial transport, Santa Cruz sugarcane and rice growers and valley residents announced road blockades against the 'dieselazo'; the government said no blockades were in force and deployed police and armed forces to prevent them.

22 Sep — Santa Cruz: A national drivers' assembly declared itself 'in emergency', demanded the decree be repealed and called a 24-hour nationwide withdrawal of transport for 28 Sep; talks with independent drivers' unions ended without agreement but with technical working groups.

Ongoing — Nationwide: The state of exception banning road blockades, extended by Congress on 17 Sep, runs to 17 Dec; Defence Minister Justiniano said peaceful protest is allowed but road closures are not, and urban teachers announced a national march for 30 Sep.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained, with upward pressure. Bringing the diesel subsidy removal forward has turned the Q4 risk flagged last week into an immediate one: transport, farm and teachers' unions are coordinating protests, and a state of exception that bans blockades sets up a direct clash if sectors try to cut roads. Over 90 days, expect staggered strikes and marches peaking around the 28–30 September actions, attempts at blockades in Santa Cruz and La Paz provinces, and possible use of force to clear roads. Negotiated partial compensation remains the government's likely off-ramp. Upgrade to CRITICAL if multi-day blockades return, security forces clash with protesters causing deaths, or Morales-aligned groups join the mobilization.

countries.name: Dominican Republic
incidents: 22 Sep — Border provinces: The General Directorate of Migration reported detaining 1,482 undocumented Haitians in operations across several provinces and deporting 484 through the Dajabon, Elias Pina, Jimani and Pedernales crossings.

23 Sep — Santo Domingo area: Police detained suspects over the home-invasion attack that wounded merengue artist Julian Oro Duro and killed his wife Zeneida Socorro Castillo; four suspects were identified and the alleged organizer was a technician who had worked for the family.

Ongoing — Nationwide: More than 370,000 undocumented Haitians have been deported in the past year, and authorities have seized more than 29 tonnes of illicit drugs in 2026, including a 595-package cocaine interdiction off Peravia on 13 Sep with US support.
countries.coa: LOW maintained. There were no significant armed-violence events in the window; high-profile crime such as the Oro Duro case is being solved quickly by police. Expect mass deportations and border-wall construction to continue at a record pace over the next 90 days, especially if the Haiti GSF vote or gang offensives trigger new displacement toward the border. The Dominican Republic's role as a Caribbean cocaine transit point and joint US interdiction will continue to generate maritime seizures. Main risks are diplomatic and humanitarian friction with Haiti rather than internal instability.

countries.name: Jamaica
incidents: 18 Sep — Seaford Town, Westmoreland: A man known as 'Pepper' was shot dead during a joint police-military operation shortly after 03:00; residents disputed the shootout account, saying he was killed at home in front of his children, and INDECOM opened an investigation.
20 Sep — Annotto Bay, St Mary: An off-duty soldier allegedly shot and killed a man at a garage following an argument.

23 Sep — Luana, St Elizabeth: Prime Minister Holness defended the security forces after the police killing of Jowayne Salmon, saying criminals were posing as innocent community members and that murders should end the year below 600.

Ongoing — Nationwide: INDECOM reported 67 people killed in 26 multiple-fatality security-force shootings in 2026, already above the 2025 total, with about 19 people killed by security forces in September by mid-month.
countries.coa: LOW maintained. Homicides remain on track for a historic low (below 600 for the year), keeping the overall threat LOW, but security-force killings (around 217 so far in 2026) and disputed accounts from residents are becoming the main source of community tension. Over 90 days, expect further contested police shootings, localized roadblock protests and INDECOM scrutiny, with the government firmly backing the security forces. Watch for any escalation of protests into sustained unrest in Kingston/St Andrew or western parishes, and for hurricane-season impacts as a parallel non-conflict hazard.
